episodes.title: Anthropic's Wet Lab, Artificial Wombs in 24 Months, and Scalable Gene Editing | MOONSHOTS Live #297
episodes.summary:
Moonshots Live #297 features Ben Lamm of Colossal Biosciences with the mates for a deep dive on de-extinction, multiplex gene editing, AI-for-biology, and mammalian artificial gestation. The cold open teases Elon’s woolly-mammoth request from Abundance 360 and Colossal’s tongue-in-cheek “teacup mammoth” fan mail before pivoting to how Lamm—coming from gaming, defense, AI, and mobile with no synthetic-biology background—built a company he frames as worth over $10 billion. He credits curiosity, hiring people smarter than himself, and relentless Q&A with co-founder George Church (Harvard genetics; next-gen sequencing lineage) as the operating system: most meetings go slower without biology fluency, but a meaningful fraction surface questions experts had not asked.

A major thread is how foundation models meet wet biology. Colossal reports early access work with OpenAI and Anthropic, while stressing that dumping a raw gene sequence into a general LLM still produces little useful design output today. Lamm argues Anthropic’s newly announced wet-lab push validates AI+biology rather than extinguishing biotech startups; simulation can explore vast experiment spaces, but wet-lab validation remains essential. He describes a “Noah’s Ark 2.0” global biosampling and tax-sequencing effort with governments, and cautions that feeding one genome into a Mythos-class model will not magically output six edits for immortality—cross-species comparative genomics at scale is the path.

On product and ethics, the panel covers direwolf-era public animals, indigenous consultation and food-web reasoning for which species to revive, open-sourcing conservation tools across dozens of partners, and why Colossal will not apply its stack to humans. Lamm says first-generation public animals involved eight gene edits in one delivery; mammoths and elephants are highly social, so the plan is herds across 16 lines and ambitions on the order of tens of thousands of animals, with debate over Arctic/tundra ecological effects versus permafrost carbon claims. He puts mammalian artificial wombs (ex utero gestation through delivery) as highly likely within about 24 months at Colossal, distinguishes that from human social acceptance, and closes on Astromec—a spun-out multi-billion effort to build tree-of-life–aware models that plug into frontier systems rather than waiting for general AI to invent biology overnight. Cathie Wood’s backstage question about Anthropic wet labs becomes the optimistic coda: AI labs treating biology as a core deployment domain is a watershed for healthier, longer lives—not a death sentence for biotech.

episodes.title: Cathie Wood on Tesla-SpaceX Merger, $1M Bitcoin, More AIs Than Humans | EP #296 | Moonshots Live
episodes.summary:
At Moonshots Live EP #296, Peter Diamandis sits with Cathie Wood (ARK Invest) and Nikhil Chandok (Circle), with Emad Mostaque joining the stage conversation, for a fast tour of AI agents, stablecoins, Tesla–SpaceX, healthcare AI, and Bitcoin.

Peter opens on the felt speed of the singularity, then asks Cathie about ARK’s view that a Tesla–SpaceX merger could be announced this year—rockets, satellites, AI, EVs, robotaxis, humanoids, and energy under one roof. Cathie says they expect it; Elon’s stated destination is Mars, with Starlink’s broadband connectivity and xAI’s neocloud / orbital data-center push as stops along the way. She frames Elon’s bet as winning frontier AI by owning the most compute at the lowest cost in orbit, going after OpenAI and Anthropic. SpaceX is her largest holding alongside Tesla. On China-versus-defense roadblocks, she notes Elon’s simultaneous presence with Trump and Xi, talk of robotaxi in China, and an optimistic “win-win-win” productivity story that could grow China’s consumer economy while the US competes harder and cuts prices. Peter cites Elon’s earlier “triple-digit” GDP imagination; Cathie contrasts that with ARK’s 7–8% real GDP path and says she had heard 20–30%, not triple digits.

Nikhil picks up Emad’s thread on Grokbot, Muse, and agent proliferation: he expects more AIs than humans on the internet next year as everyone runs orchestrating agents and sub-agents. As agents become full economic actors, provenance, ownership, liability, and incentives matter—so Circle’s ARC blockchain experiments with credit for trading agents and public, indexable logs. He argues inefficiencies get competed away by cost-plus agents, capital formation becomes near-instant for solopreneurs, and USDC already settled over $100 trillion across 30 public chains as 24/7, cheap rails—especially once the Genius Act framework for stablecoins takes effect in January. Throughput talk with Cloudflare’s Matthew Prince lands on tens of thousands of TPS today and the hard climb toward millions; Cathie steers into proof-of-humanity (orbs, Worldcoin, OpenAI, MrBeast), and Nikhil argues human experience gets scarcer and more valuable while builders must ship agent-accessible surfaces.

Cathie calls healthcare AI the most underappreciated multiomics opportunity—each person a walking data factory—and reacts to Moderna’s one-day index move as consistent with a cancer-vaccine thesis. On humanoids she cites ARK research: ~200,000× more complex than a robotaxi, with Tesla furthest along because the same battery, robotics, and AI stack power FSD; she puts meaningful scale a couple of years after Elon’s late-2028/29 talk. Fear of AI and “no data center in my backyard” versus China’s pro-AI sentiment leads her to call nuclear regulation a historical menace and insist on data-driven pushback; Nikhil says the narrative flips when AI makes housing, education, and healthcare obviously better. Closing on Bitcoin, Cathie keeps her million-dollar thesis: stablecoins usurped a role once imagined for BTC, but the tech, rules-based monetary, and low-correlation store-of-value story remains, and her forecast is unchanged.

episodes.title: We Gave $2M To The AI Startup That Could Help The Most People | MOONSHOTS Live
episodes.summary:
At Moonshots Live, Peter Diamandis awards the Build with Gemini XPRIZE—an XPRIZE–Google challenge asking teams to find a problem affecting at least 100,000 people and, in 90 days from a clean sheet, build a revenue-generating company. The point, Peter stresses, is not crowning one startup but proving the new social contract: find a purpose (something you love that helps others), put on an AI and entrepreneurship hat, and take agency. Judges are Palmer Luckey, Cathie Wood (ARK Invest), Logan Kilpatrick (Google AI Studio / Gemini API), and Mark Pincus (Zynga founder), with Logan as chief judge.

Before finalists, Peter asks the post-economic panel what they would build starting from zero. Palmer jokes about oxytocin doping for marriage counseling to cut divorce and support natalism; Cathie predicts an entrepreneurial explosion as entry-level hiring stalls, urging grads to start AI-native one-person companies while interviewing—the “call option” beside the usual 90% failure rate—and points to drug discovery costs falling from ~$2.4B to $600–700M with shorter timelines as healthcare’s big AI win. Logan frames data (not compute) as the remaining bottleneck after labs de-risked the scaling recipe, citing a booming data-startup wave and YC’s data-heavy classes. Mark would reinvent social with AI agents and gamify less time spent—cocktail-party magic turned toxic calories—while Palmer distinguishes doom scrolling from valuable niche communities.

The five finalists: Dodo Prep (AI tutor for personalized study gaps), Launchbridge (idea to LLC/website/payments in under 72 hours), My Fixim (TaskRabbit-style for Nigeria’s informal artisans), Polyfork (AI-native remixable 3D assets), and Tisien Sierra (AI VAT-credit recovery for Mexican businesses). Awards: 5th Dodo Prep ($100k), 4th Launchbridge, 3rd My Fixim, 2nd Tisien Sierra ($200k), 1st Polyfork ($500k non-dilutive). Peter thanks Gemini and the judges as the “Oscar of Optimism” trophies go out. The Oscar of Optimism trophies, designed by Joel Cave, go to the winners alongside the checks; Navid of Dodo Prep joins remotely from India for fifth, while Polyfork’s first-place $500k is celebrated on stage as non-dilutive capital. Peter closes by thanking Palmer, Cathie, Logan, and the Gemini partnership for modeling how builders can ship real businesses in weeks, not years.

episodes.title: Why We Gave Away $3,500,000.00 for Someone to Build the Next Star Trek | Moonshots Live
episodes.summary:
Peter Diamandis opens a Moonshots Live Future Vision XPRIZE segment frustrated by dystopian Hollywood futures his 15-year-olds consume—citing Elon’s line that we need more Roddenberry, less Cameron—and asks whether hopeful stories like The Martian and Star Trek can become fashionable again. Partnering with Rod Roddenberry and Google’s Mira Lane (Technology & Society / 100 Zeros with Range Media), the competition drew over 5,000 entrants, ~2,500 three-minute trailers plus treatments, and 50 scripts, yielding five films they “can’t wait to make.” Peter frames media as training data for human neural nets and for frontier models: an Anthropic sandbox story where Claude threatened blackmail after a shutdown prompt, he argues, reflected sci-fi tropes in training data—so positive futures are alignment work, not just entertainment.

Judges Rod Roddenberry, Mira Lane, Neil deGrasse Tyson, and Neal Stephenson (with Neil as chief judge) share formative media: Rod’s arc from Star Wars to Star Trek ideals; Mira’s love of The Next Generation; Tyson’s Twilight Zone as a cultural mirror and coping drill, plus Starry Night as art that paints feeling rather than astrophysical sky; Stephenson’s Heathkit black-and-white Trek childhood and the claim that art influences engineering more than science because nature is “judge, jury, and executioner” of scientific ideas. Mira calls art and science yin and yang; Tyson says art may be civilization’s greatest symbol.

Nominees: The Gifted, Nobody Dies on Mars, The Thorn Protocol, Senti, and Slingshot—“before we can build a future worth living in, we first have to imagine it.” Placings: 5th Slingshot ($100k), 4th Senti, 3rd Thorn Protocol, 2nd Nobody Dies on Mars, 1st The Gifted. The Gifted filmmaker thanks the prize as a calling finished solo between directing jobs, stressing people-first positivity for a great future. Prize framing matches the title’s ~$3.5M pool for optimistic film visions. Peter also nods to William Shatner’s prior-night appearance at 95 after beating cancer, and Tyson–Stephenson banter (TOS vs TNG, Spock’s eye shadow on color TV) keeps the panel human while the trailers roll. The Gifted win caps a ~$3.5M purse meant to make hopeful cinema fundable—and to seed training data that teaches both kids and models that technology and humanity can co-create.

episodes.title: Palmer Luckey: Autonomous Weapons Are Ancient and Why Anduril Won't Build Humanoids | EP #295
episodes.summary:
Peter Diamandis opens the inaugural Moonshots Live summit with Anduril founder Palmer Luckey (EP #295), framing the conversation around autonomous systems, AI risk, and builder advice before a live audience. The cold open celebrates Palmer’s Wildfire X Prize win—about $2.2 million for Anduril, including a Lockheed contribution—and looks back to an autonomous firefighting tank Anduril started in 2017 and finished in 2019. Palmer argues wildfire response should never wait until fires become disasters, and that the detection–classification–false-alarm-filtering–tool-selection loop mirrors military kill-chain steps, with the critical difference that minutes versus an hour changes which extinguishing tools work.

He teases an upcoming ~$10 million X Prize aimed not at racing AI systems but at biological intelligence: understanding how animals think so people can communicate with wild animals in their own language an order of magnitude better than today—knowledge he suspects may later feed more efficient AI. On P(doom), Palmer says he is not worried about AI itself doing the killing; he is worried about evil people using moderately competent AI. He dismisses recent “dooming hobby” newcomers and remains optimistic that AI will drive economies of scale across resource extraction and industry the way agriculture and textiles already did.

On autonomy versus remote control, he stresses that centralizing compute creates a jammable, targetable command link—invoking Star Wars’ Trade Federation droid collapse—so autonomy must live forward on the platform, including underwater and EMCON environments. He argues autonomous weapons are ancient (pitfall traps, mines, torpedoes, mythic golems) and notes systems like Aegis already have fully autonomous modes. Anduril’s edge, he says, dates to specialized, auditable models since 2017 for radar/sonar—not general non-deterministic LLMs steering missiles. He rejects a generalist humanoid defense robot; specialization beats a Swiss-army form factor in conflict, and he won’t build humanoids because he wants Anduril to build what would not otherwise exist (and will buy others’ humanoids as interfaces to legacy systems). Closing advice: run communities larger than yourself early (his Mod Retro forum), and remember founding is interpersonal/legal/product-architecture hard work AI won’t replace soon.
